difficultyRationale: Each statement checks a different fact about stream pipelines: laziness, single use, stateful operations, short-circuiting and the purpose of peek.
prompt: Which statements about Java streams are true? Select all that apply.
explanation: A pipeline does no work until a terminal operation starts it, and a stream can be consumed only once. Operations such as sorted are stateful: they may need to see the whole input before producing output. limit is a short-circuiting intermediate operation, not a terminal one, and peek exists mainly to support debugging.

options.text: An intermediate operation such as `filter` does not process any element until a terminal operation is invoked.
options.explanation: Intermediate operations are lazy. Traversal of the source starts only when the terminal operation is executed.

options.text: The same `Stream` instance can be traversed a second time after its terminal operation has completed.
options.explanation: A stream must be operated on only once. Reusing it throws IllegalStateException; a new stream must be created from the source.
Sorting needs to see all the elements before it can emit the first one in order, which is the definition of a stateful operation.
limit returns a stream, so it is an intermediate operation. It is short-circuiting because it can finish the traversal early.

options.text: `peek` exists mainly to support debugging, for example to see elements as they flow past a point in the pipeline.
options.explanation: The API documentation describes this as the main purpose of peek. It should not be relied on for side effects that matter.
